audits.derivedAnswer: A: 6. The exact shaded area after 100 stages is 6(1 − 4^(−100)) square units.
audits.mathematicalReason: The original right triangle has area 6·6/2 = 18. The first shaded triangle BCD has perpendicular legs 3 and 3, so its area is 9/2. Each subsequent subdivision halves corresponding lengths, making each new shaded area one quarter of its predecessor. Thus S_100 = (9/2)(1 − (1/4)^100)/(1 − 1/4) = 6(1 − 4^(−100)), whose nearest listed value is 6. Similar-triangle area scaling and finite geometric summation are valid assessed scopes, supported by midpoint and triangle-area facts.

figureEvidence.fact: The first three shaded regions are triangles BCD, KDE, and LEF. Subdivision continues in the successively smaller corner triangles toward G; it is not applied simultaneously to every unshaded triangle.

audits.mathematicalReason: The semicircle has diameter BD = 10. Each radius-5 quarter-circle has chord length 5√2, so AB = AD = 5√2. Consequently A lies 5 units below the midpoint of BD. Complete the 10-by-5 rectangle below BD: its lower corners are the centers of the two quarter-circles. The required area is the rectangle plus the upper semicircle minus the two quarter-disks: 50 + 25π/2 − 2(25π/4) = 50. This directly supports the sector-area scope and rectangle-area support.

figureEvidence.fact: Arc BCD forms the boundary above chord BD. The two inward-curving quarter-circle boundaries AB and AD lie below BD and meet at A, establishing which circular pieces must be added and subtracted.

audits.derivedAnswer: B: 1 quantity changes; only the perimeter is nonconstant.
audits.mathematicalReason: Let AB = b and let the fixed distance between AB and P's parallel line be h. The midpoint theorem gives MN = b/2. The triangle area is bh/2. The trapezoid has parallel bases b and b/2 separated by h/2, so its area is (b + b/2)(h/2)/2 = 3bh/8. These three quantities are constant. If A = (0,0), B = (b,0), and P = (x,h), the perimeter is b + √(x²+h²) + √((x−b)²+h²), which is nonconstant in x. The candidate's three assessed scopes form a valid direct method; the trapezoid formula need not be required of alternative methods.

figureEvidence.fact: A and B form the fixed base, P moves on the separate line parallel to AB, and the midpoint segment MN cuts off trapezoid ABNM below it.

audits.mathematicalReason: The rays occur in the order DA, DP, DB, DC, so ∠ADP = 30° and ∠ADB = 60°. Since AD = 1, right-triangle calculations give DB = 1/cos 60° = 2, DP = 1/cos 30° = 2√3/3, AB = tan 60° = √3, and AP = tan 30° = √3/3. Hence PB = AB − AP = 2√3/3, and the perimeter is 2 + 4√3/3. The geometric route is also valid: ∠PBD = ∠PDB = 30° gives PB = DP, while the 30°-triangle property and Pythagoras determine the lengths. Trigonometry is a valid selected method, not a universally necessary one.

figureEvidence.fact: P lies between A and B on the top side of the rectangle. From D, DP lies between DA and DB, and DB lies between DP and DC; this fixes the order of the three 30° sectors.

audits.mathematicalReason: The three-digit integer powers of 5 are 125 and 625, both with tens digit 2. The three-digit integer powers of 2 are 128, 256, and 512. The crossing requires the across entry's hundreds digit to equal the down entry's tens digit, so the across entry must be 256. Its units digit, in the outlined square, is therefore 6. Computing powers and identifying decimal places are both directly assessed by this method.

figureEvidence.fact: The first square of the three-cell across entry is the middle square of the three-cell down entry. The outlined square is the rightmost, or units, square of the across entry.

audits.mathematicalReason: Each of the seven 100-foot courses needs at least 50 blocks. A course with exactly 50 blocks consists entirely of 2-foot blocks and has internal joins at 2, 4, …, 98 feet. Two such courses cannot be adjacent. Thus at most four courses can use 50 blocks, and at least three need 51 or more, giving a universal lower bound of 4·50 + 3·51 = 353. Attain it by alternating four all-2-foot courses with three courses consisting of a 1-foot block, forty-nine 2-foot blocks, and a final 1-foot block. The latter courses have joins at odd positions, so adjacent joins do not align and both wall ends are even. The bound-and-construction scope is fully supported.

figureEvidence.fact: The illustrated adjacent courses have offset vertical joins, with a short end block shifting one course's joins relative to the other. The sketch illustrates staggering; its unequal right endpoints are not treated as the ends of the completed wall.

audits.mathematicalReason: Tangency gives OA perpendicular to AB. In the nondegenerate configuration, 0 < θ < π/2, and OA = 1 gives AB = tan θ and OB = sec θ. Set OC = x, so AC = 1 − x. The internal angle-bisector theorem gives AC/OC = AB/OB = sin θ. Therefore 1 − x = x sin θ and x = 1/(1 + sin θ). The equal-distance route independently gives the same equation: the distance from C to BA is 1 − x, while its perpendicular distance to BO is x sin θ. Both proposed routes are valid, and the result lies between 1/2 and 1, consistent with C lying inside OA.

figureEvidence.fact: O, C, and A are collinear in that order, B is outside the circle, and the marked right angle is between OA and AB. The marked angle θ is between OA and OB.

audits.mathematicalReason: Assigning eight distinct colors to eight labeled faces gives 8! colorings. The regular octahedron has 24 rotational symmetries: a fixed face has eight possible image faces, with three possible cyclic orientations on each. Because all face colors are distinct, no nonidentity rotation fixes a coloring, so every rotational orbit has size 24. The required count is 8!/24 = 1680. Reflections are not identified. This is precisely symmetry counting, supported by permutations and the multiplication principle.

figureEvidence.fact: The drawing depicts the triangular-faced octahedron, with four edges meeting at each vertex. It is used to identify the solid's face and rotation geometry, not to infer lengths or angles from the perspective projection.
